n: Job gives his final reply to the Lord — humble, honest, and transformed.
Job confesses that God can do anything and that no purpose of his can be stopped.

f.w: no thought can be withholden from thee
f.g: No plan of yours can be thwarted.

n: Quoting God’s question (38:2), Job admits he spoke of things he didn’t understand — wonders beyond his knowledge.

f.w: Who is he that hideth counsel without knowledge?

n: He quotes God again (38:3; 40:7): “Listen, and I will question you.” Job now takes the role of the learner.

f.w: I will demand of thee, and declare thou unto me

n: The turning point of the book: Job had known about God by hearsay, but now he has seen God for himself. Personal revelation has replaced secondhand religion.
So Job retracts his complaints and repents in dust and ashes. He isn’t confessing hidden sins — he is humbly yielding his demand that God explain himself.

f.g: Or “I retract my words” — the Hebrew can mean reject or recant.

n: The prose story resumes. The Lord tells Eliphaz he is angry with him and his two friends, because they didn’t speak rightly about God as Job did. Honest wrestling pleased God more than pious falsehood.

f.w: ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right

n: The friends must offer seven bulls and seven rams and ask Job to pray for them. God will accept Job’s prayer and spare them. Job, once condemned by them, becomes their intercessor — a type of Christ.

f.w: my servant Job shall pray for you

f.g: An offering entirely burned on the altar, symbolizing complete dedication and atonement.

n: The three friends obey, and the Lord accepts Job’s prayer.

f.g: Literally “lifted up Job’s face” — showed him favor.

n: The Lord restores Job’s fortunes after he prays for his friends — and gives him twice as much as before. Forgiving those who hurt him comes before the blessing.
His family and old friends finally come, eat with him, and comfort him, each giving a piece of silver and a gold ring.

f.g: Hebrew qesitah, an ancient unit of value, also mentioned in Genesis 33:19.

n: The Lord blesses Job’s later life more than his early life. His herds are exactly double those in 1:3.

He has seven sons and three daughters again — the same number as before. Many note that his children are not “doubled” because his first children were not lost forever; Latter-day Saints believe families can continue beyond death.
Unusually, the daughters are named: Jemimah (“dove”), Keziah (“cassia,” a fragrant spice), and Keren-happuch (“horn of eye-paint”).

f.g: Horn (container) of eye cosmetic — a symbol of beauty.

n: Job’s daughters were the most beautiful in the land, and remarkably he gave them an inheritance alongside their brothers — a rare act of generosity and honor for women in that era.

f.w: gave them inheritance among their brethren

n: Job lives 140 more years and sees four generations of descendants.
Job dies old and full of days — a satisfying, complete life. His story teaches that faith can survive suffering without having every question answered.
